title: XML Media Types
summary: Standardizes the media types text/xml, application/xml, and related types for exchanging XML, plus the +xml suffix convention for naming XML-based types. It tells software how to label and handle XML content. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 7303.

eli5.summary: Files need labels so computers know how to open them. This gives XML files their official labels and a trick for naming new kinds. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: what is the mime type for xml
what is the default charset for text/xml
subtitle: The official media type labels for XML, plus the +xml suffix for naming XML-based formats.

tldr.problem: XML was being exchanged on the Web and in WebDAV, but there was no proper media type to label it, and labeling it as SGML was inappropriate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers five media types (text/xml, application/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd), explains how the charset parameter works, and recommends a +xml suffix for other XML-based types.
tldr.outcome: The +xml convention let generic XML tools recognize any XML-based type. RFC 3023 was obsoleted by RFC 7303 and later updated by RFC 6839.

today: RFC 3023 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7303 and updated by RFC 6839, so RFC 7303 is the one to read for the current rules. It obsoleted RFC 2376 and updated RFC 2048.

sections.title: Why XML Needed Its Own Types
sections.content:
The W3C had issued XML 1.0 (Second Edition), and XML network entities were already being exchanged on the Web and used by the WebDAV protocol. A media type was needed to label them properly.

XML is a subset of SGML, which already had text/sgml and application/sgml. The RFC gives three reasons not to reuse them. Many applications can process XML but not the larger SGML. SGML applications cannot always process XML entities. And the SGML types define parameters that XML does not use, which would be ambiguous. So XML gets new types in the IETF tree.

The RFC also introduces the term XML MIME entity: an XML entity wrapped inside a MIME entity, since MIME and XML use the word entity differently.
sections.eli5: XML looks like an older kind of file, but it behaves differently. So it needed its own name tag instead of borrowing the old one.

sections.title: The Five Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers text/xml, application/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd. The first two MAY label XML "document entities". The external parsed entity types SHOULD label external parsed entities, and application/xml-dtd SHOULD label external DTD subsets or external parameter entities. The two document types MUST NOT be used for DTD subsets or parameter entities.

Choosing between text/ and application/ is about readers. If the source XML is readable by casual users, text/xml is preferable, since software that does not know it treats it as text/plain. Otherwise use application/xml. If unsure, the RFC suggests the conservative choice of application/*.

All five have an optional charset parameter, which is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED. Suggested file extensions include .xml, .ent, .dtd and .mod.
sections.eli5: There are five labels for different kinds of XML pieces. Pick the "text" label if a person can read it comfortably, and the "application" label if it is mostly for programs.

sections.title: Charsets and the Byte Order Mark
sections.content:
The charset parameter is authoritative: it wins over any encoding declaration inside the document. For text/xml, if charset is omitted, MIME and XML processors MUST use us-ascii, even over HTTP, overriding the ISO-8859-1 default of HTTP/1.1. For application/xml with no charset, conforming XML processors follow section 4.3.3 of the XML specification, and other MIME processors SHOULD NOT assume a default. utf-8 is the recommended value.

The UTF-16 family (utf-16, utf-16le, utf-16be) is not allowed under the text top-level type except over HTTP. A utf-16 entity MUST begin with a byte order mark (BOM), 0xFE 0xFF or 0xFF 0xFE, and converters MUST strip it when going to a non-Unicode encoding and add it when going to utf-16. The utf-16le and utf-16be charsets MUST NOT begin with a BOM. Gateways from HTTP to other MIME applications MUST turn text/xml; charset="utf-16" into application/xml; charset="utf-16".
sections.eli5: The label on the box says which alphabet code the letters inside use, and the label is the boss. If there is no label on a "text" box, assume the plainest code, US-ASCII.

sections.title: The +xml Naming Convention
sections.content:
New media types for XML-based formats SHOULD end with +xml, for example application/mathml+xml, application/rdf+xml or image/svg+xml. Tools can match the pattern */*+xml to know a type is XML, then use generic XML processing for browsing, editing, fragment identification, linking, searching, storage and well-formedness checking.

Registrants SHOULD use the suffix unless they have a compelling reason not to, such as wanting a type to stay opaque to generic tools. Subtypes that are not XML MIME entities MUST NOT register with the suffix. The RFC updates the registration process of RFC 2048 accordingly. New XML-based registrations under text should refer to text/xml for charset and encoding, and others to application/xml.

HTTP does not support an Accept: */*+xml header, so it MUST NOT be used that way.
sections.eli5: Imagine every new kind of XML file ends its name with +xml, like a family surname. Anyone seeing the surname knows it belongs to the XML family.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML has all the security considerations of SGML as described in RFC 1874, and likely more. XML entities may contain data that a system executes, so recipients may be at risk. Any information stored outside the user's control, such as style sheets, XSL transformations, entity declarations and DTDs, can be a source of insecurity. A small "whiteout attack" change to a master style sheet could make words disappear, and a broken DTD could halt processing on a large scale. The security of a document depends on every document it references, recursively.

The RFC also describes entity spoofing, where the first of several entity declarations wins, and notes that XML can contain escape sequences that change the display environment. Display processors SHOULD filter these or reset settings, and the ability to program keys SHOULD be blocked. Recursive entity expansion is prohibited by the XML specification, but even non-recursive expansion repeated many times can strain computing resources.
sections.eli5: A page can borrow pieces from other places, so if someone sneaks a bad piece in, your page looks wrong or does something nasty. Be careful what you trust.

sections.title: Examples and Changes
sections.content:
Section 8 gives worked Content-type examples, such as text/xml; charset="utf-8", UTF-16 with a BOM, and an omitted charset. It also shows +xml types like application/mathml+xml and image/svg+xml. Section 5 and 6 note that fragment identifiers and base URIs for XML were still being defined by W3C work at the time.

The major differences from RFC 2376 are the three added types (text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd), the +xml suffix convention, and the discussion of utf-16le and utf-16be.
sections.eli5: This is the new, bigger label book. It has three more labels, the +xml surname trick and some sample labels.
